expectedText:
PARTITION ACTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan and Casey Morgan

DECLARATION OF CO-OWNERSHIP INTEREST AND CONTEMPLATED PARTITION RELIEF
Jordan Alex Lee states the following regarding real property located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, described as Lot 12, Block 3, Tract No. 4567, as per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County Records (the "Property"), also identified by Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789, provided for identification only and not as part of the Property's legal description.

Jordan Alex Lee holds an interest in the Property as a co-owner, together with Taylor Morgan and Casey Morgan, under a form of concurrent ownership described as tenants in common.

Jordan Alex Lee is considering, or intends to pursue, a partition action under California Code of Civil Procedure Title 10.5 (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 872.010-874.323), seeking partition by sale of the Property.

This declaration states Jordan Alex Lee's own description of the Property, the co-ownership at issue, and the type of partition relief being considered; it does not itself divide, sell, or transfer any interest in the Property, and does not determine any co-owner's rights in the Property, which are decided by a court in a partition action, not by this document.

WHO MAY BRING A PARTITION ACTION, AND THE PROPERTY INTERESTS IT COVERS
California's partition statute states specifically who may commence and maintain a partition action: a coowner of personal property, or an owner of an estate of inheritance, an estate for life, or an estate for years in real property where that property or estate is owned by several persons concurrently or in successive estates. The statute's own text does not use the phrases "tenants in common" or "joint tenants"; it instead describes the covered ownership generally, as real property or an estate in real property owned by several persons concurrently (or in successive estates). Concurrent ownership of an estate in real property by several persons is the general category that both tenancy in common and joint tenancy fall within, but this clause does not evaluate whether a specific form of co-ownership, or a specific person's interest, in fact qualifies. Separately, the statute's governing title states that it governs actions for partition of real property and, except to the extent not applicable, actions for partition of personal property as well — a partition action is therefore not limited to real estate. The statute also contains an express carve-out: notwithstanding the persons and interests just described, an action between spouses or putative spouses for partition of their community or quasi-community property, or their quasi-marital interest in property, may not be commenced or maintained under this title.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

(2) An owner of an estate of inheritance, an estate for life, or an estate for years in real property where such property or estate therein is owned by several persons concurrently or in successive estates. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), an action between spouses or putative spouses for partition of their community or quasi-community property or their quasi-marital interest in property may not be commenced or maintained under this title."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.210(a)-(b), California Code of Civil Procedure, Partition of Real and Personal Property, persons who may bring a partition action and the spousal community property carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=872.210.)
  "This title governs actions for partition of real property and, except to the extent not applicable, actions for partition of personal property."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.020, California Code of Civil Procedure, Partition of Real and Personal Property, scope of the governing title (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=872.020.)
  Known gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.210, subdivisions (a) and (b), are subsections of a single statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independent sources; Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.020 is a genuinely separate, independently numbered section and is treated as an independent source from § 872.210. This clause does not evaluate whether spouses or putative spouses seeking to divide community or quasi-community real property have an alternative remedy, such as under the Family Code, which this document does not address. This clause states only who is statutorily entitled to bring the action and what property interests are covered in general terms; it does not evaluate the sufficiency of any specific person's claimed interest, the classification of any specific property as separate or community property, or whether a specific co-ownership arrangement is a tenancy in common, a joint tenancy, or some other form of concurrent ownership. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on who may bring a partition action and what it covers — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific co-ownership dispute; other states' partition statutes, if any, may define eligible parties and covered property differently.

THE COURT'S EQUITABLE POWER TO ORDER ACCOUNTING AND CONTRIBUTION AMONG CO-OWNERS
California's partition statute gives the court a general equitable power, applicable to every partition action, to address financial imbalances among co-owners: "The court may, in all cases, order allowance, accounting, contribution, or other compensatory adjustment among the parties according to the principles of equity." This is the statutory hook that allows a partition court to take into account, as part of resolving the action, that one co-owner may have paid more than a proportionate share of expenses associated with the property, or received more than a proportionate share of its benefits, while the property was jointly owned. The statute's own text is general: it does not itself list or define specific categories of expense (such as property taxes, mortgage payments, or the cost of necessary repairs) or benefit (such as rental income or exclusive use) that qualify for an accounting or contribution award. It instead commits that determination, category by category and case by case, to the court's application of "the principles of equity."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The court may, in all cases, order allowance, accounting, contribution, or other compensatory adjustment among the parties according to the principles of equity."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.140, California Code of Civil Procedure, Partition of Real and Personal Property, court's equitable power over accounting, contribution, and compensatory adjustment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=872.140.)
  Known gap: This clause is based on a single statutory section, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.140. It states only that this general equitable power exists; it does not itself enumerate which categories of expense or benefit a court has treated as subject to contribution or accounting under this section, does not research or cite the case law that has applied "the principles of equity" to specific categories of expense in a partition action, and does not evaluate whether an accounting, contribution, or other compensatory adjustment would be available, or in what amount, on the facts of any specific co-ownership dispute. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a California partition court holds this general equitable power — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property dispute; other states' partition statutes, if any, may state this power differently or not at all.

COSTS OF PARTITION, INCLUDING ATTORNEY'S FEES, AND HOW THEY ARE APPORTIONED
California's partition statute states its own, specific rule for attorney's fees in a partition action, distinct from the general default rule (sometimes called the "American Rule") under which each party bears its own attorney's fees absent a statute or contract providing otherwise. The partition statute defines a category called "costs of partition," which by its own terms includes "[r]easonable attorney's fees incurred or paid by a party for the common benefit," along with other listed items such as a referee's fee and the cost of a title report. Having defined that category, the statute then states the default rule for dividing it among the parties: "Except as otherwise provided in this article, the court shall apportion the costs of partition among the parties in proportion to their interests or make such other apportionment as may be equitable." Where the action is governed by California's Partition of Real Property Act (addressed in a separate clause of this document), an added, more specific limitation applies to that apportionment: the court "may apportion the costs of partition, including an appraisal fee," under this same proportion-or-equity standard, "except that the court shall not apportion the costs of partition to any party that opposes the partition unless doing so is equitable and consistent with the purposes of this chapter."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

  "Except as otherwise provided in this article, the court shall apportion the costs of partition among the parties in proportion to their interests or make such other apportionment as may be equitable."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 874.040, California Code of Civil Procedure, treated as related to, not independent of, § 874.010 above; default apportionment of costs of partition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=874.040.)
  "In an action for partition of property, the court may apportion the costs of partition, including an appraisal fee, pursuant to Section 874.040, except that the court shall not apportion the costs of partition to any party that opposes the partition unless doing so is equitable and consistent with the purposes of this chapter."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 874.321.5, California Code of Civil Procedure, Partition of Real Property Act, added limitation on apportioning costs against a party who opposes partition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=874.321.5.)

Proc. § 874.321.5 is a genuinely separate, independently numbered section in a different chapter (Chapter 10, added in 2021 and amended in 2022) that by its own text cross-references and narrows § 874.040's apportionment standard; it is treated as an independent source from §§ 874.010 and 874.040, though the three provisions operate together. This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of § 874.010's list of items included in "costs of partition"; the remaining items in that same subdivision, and the entire remainder of Chapter 8, are not independently quoted or fully described here. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific attorney's fees were in fact incurred "for the common benefit," does not evaluate what apportionment would be equitable on the facts of any specific action, and does not evaluate whether § 874.321.5's added limitation applies to any specific party or action. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's cost-and-fee-allocation rule for a partition action — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dispute; other states' partition statutes, if any, may allocate attorney's fees and costs differently, including by following the general American Rule with no partition-specific exception.

PARTITION IN KIND VS. PARTITION BY SALE: THE STATUTORY PREFERENCE AND THE "GREAT PREJUDICE" STANDARD
Under California's Partition of Real Property Act (addressed in a separate clause of this document as to when it applies), the statute states an explicit preference for one of the two basic forms of partition relief. Once a determination of value has been made and any statutory buyout process has concluded, "the court shall order partition in kind unless the court, after consideration of the factors listed in Section 874.319, finds that partition in kind will result in great prejudice to the cotenants as a group." Partition in kind — physical division of the property into separately titled parcels — is therefore the statute's default outcome; partition by sale is available only if the court affirmatively finds, after weighing the statutory factors, that dividing the property in kind would cause great prejudice to the cotenants as a group. Those factors include, among others, "[w]hether the property practicably can be divided among the cotenants," and "[w]hether partition in kind would apportion the property in such a way that the aggregate fair market value of the parcels resulting from the division would be materially less than the value of the property if it were sold as a whole, taking into account the condition under which a court-ordered sale likely would occur." The statute also directs the court to consider "[t]he degree to which the cotenants have contributed their pro rata share of the property taxes, insurance, and other expenses associated with maintaining ownership of the property or have contributed to the physical improvement, maintenance, or upkeep of the property." Finally, the statute states that no single factor controls this determination on its own: "The court shall not consider any one factor in subdivision (a) to be dispositive without weighing the totality of all relevant factors and circumstances."

THE PARTITION OF REAL PROPERTY ACT: WHEN ITS PROCEDURES APPLY BY DEFAULT, AND THEIR LIMIT TO TENANCY IN COMMON
In 2021 and 2022, California enacted and then substantially amended Chapter 10 of its partition title, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 874.311-874.323, titled the "Partition of Real Property Act" — California's version of a uniform act commonly associated with protecting "heirs property." The statute's own scope provision, however, is not limited by its terms to inherited property or to family heirs: it "applies to real property held in tenancy in common where there is no agreement in a record binding all the cotenants which governs the partition of the property," and it "applies to actions for partition of real property filed on or after January 1, 2023." The statute then makes this chapter's procedures — including the appraisal, buyout right, and partition-in-kind preference described elsewhere in this document — the default rule, not merely an optional or narrow add-on: "In an action to partition real property, the property shall be partitioned under this chapter unless all of the cotenants otherwise agree in a record," and, where this chapter governs, it "shall control over any provisions of this title that are inconsistent with this chapter." In other words, for a real property partition action among tenants in common filed on or after January 1, 2023, this chapter's procedures apply by default unless every cotenant has agreed, in a record, to a different partition arrangement.

UNDER THE PARTITION OF REAL PROPERTY ACT: COURT-ORDERED APPRAISAL, AND A CO-OWNER'S RIGHT TO BUY OUT COTENANTS WHO REQUESTED SALE
Where California's Partition of Real Property Act applies (addressed in a separate clause of this document), the statute builds in a valuation step and a buyout opportunity before the court decides between partition in kind and partition by sale. On valuation: "Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), the court shall determine the fair market value of the property by ordering an appraisal," and where an appraisal is ordered, "the court shall appoint a disinterested real estate appraiser licensed in the State of California to determine the fair market value of the property assuming sole ownership of the fee simple estate." Once that value has been determined, and if any cotenant has requested partition by sale, the statute gives every other cotenant — meaning a cotenant who did not request sale — a statutory opportunity to buy out the interests of the cotenants who did request sale, before any forced sale occurs: "the court shall... send notice to the parties that any cotenant except a cotenant that requested partition by sale may buy all the interests of the cotenants that requested partition by sale," and "[n]ot later than 45 days after the notice is sent... any cotenant except a cotenant that requested partition by sale may give notice to the court that it elects to buy all the interests of the cotenants that requested partition by sale." The statute elsewhere sets the buyout price at the court-determined value multiplied by the electing cotenant's fractional ownership, and provides further rules for what happens when more than one cotenant elects to buy, or when an electing cotenant fails to pay.

expectedJSON.body: Under California's Partition of Real Property Act (addressed in a separate clause of this document as to when it applies), the statute states an explicit preference for one of the two basic forms of partition relief. Once a determination of value has been made and any statutory buyout process has concluded, "the court shall order partition in kind unless the court, after consideration of the factors listed in Section 874.319, finds that partition in kind will result in great prejudice to the cotenants as a group." Partition in kind — physical division of the property into separately titled parcels — is therefore the statute's default outcome; partition by sale is available only if the court affirmatively finds, after weighing the statutory factors, that dividing the property in kind would cause great prejudice to the cotenants as a group. Those factors include, among others, "[w]hether the property practicably can be divided among the cotenants," and "[w]hether partition in kind would apportion the property in such a way that the aggregate fair market value of the parcels resulting from the division would be materially less than the value of the property if it were sold as a whole, taking into account the condition under which a court-ordered sale likely would occur." The statute also directs the court to consider "[t]he degree to which the cotenants have contributed their pro rata share of the property taxes, insurance, and other expenses associated with maintaining ownership of the property or have contributed to the physical improvement, maintenance, or upkeep of the property." Finally, the statute states that no single factor controls this determination on its own: "The court shall not consider any one factor in subdivision (a) to be dispositive without weighing the totality of all relevant factors and circumstances."

expectedJSON.body: In 2021 and 2022, California enacted and then substantially amended Chapter 10 of its partition title, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 874.311-874.323, titled the "Partition of Real Property Act" — California's version of a uniform act commonly associated with protecting "heirs property." The statute's own scope provision, however, is not limited by its terms to inherited property or to family heirs: it "applies to real property held in tenancy in common where there is no agreement in a record binding all the cotenants which governs the partition of the property," and it "applies to actions for partition of real property filed on or after January 1, 2023." The statute then makes this chapter's procedures — including the appraisal, buyout right, and partition-in-kind preference described elsewhere in this document — the default rule, not merely an optional or narrow add-on: "In an action to partition real property, the property shall be partitioned under this chapter unless all of the cotenants otherwise agree in a record," and, where this chapter governs, it "shall control over any provisions of this title that are inconsistent with this chapter." In other words, for a real property partition action among tenants in common filed on or after January 1, 2023, this chapter's procedures apply by default unless every cotenant has agreed, in a record, to a different partition arrangement.

expectedJSON.body: Where California's Partition of Real Property Act applies (addressed in a separate clause of this document), the statute builds in a valuation step and a buyout opportunity before the court decides between partition in kind and partition by sale. On valuation: "Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), the court shall determine the fair market value of the property by ordering an appraisal," and where an appraisal is ordered, "the court shall appoint a disinterested real estate appraiser licensed in the State of California to determine the fair market value of the property assuming sole ownership of the fee simple estate." Once that value has been determined, and if any cotenant has requested partition by sale, the statute gives every other cotenant — meaning a cotenant who did not request sale — a statutory opportunity to buy out the interests of the cotenants who did request sale, before any forced sale occurs: "the court shall... send notice to the parties that any cotenant except a cotenant that requested partition by sale may buy all the interests of the cotenants that requested partition by sale," and "[n]ot later than 45 days after the notice is sent... any cotenant except a cotenant that requested partition by sale may give notice to the court that it elects to buy all the interests of the cotenants that requested partition by sale." The statute elsewhere sets the buyout price at the court-determined value multiplied by the electing cotenant's fractional ownership, and provides further rules for what happens when more than one cotenant elects to buy, or when an electing cotenant fails to pay.
